To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the flux rates of O3 and of NO2 into leaves are best explained by models that include stomatal conductance (Gs) as a variable and 2) the best-fit model explaining the flux of NO2 into the leaves included stomatal conductane, apoplastic concentrations of ascorbate, NR activity and the removal rate for nitrate from the apoplast.
the flux of O(3), and the flux of NO(2), into leaves is controlled by stomatal conductances, apoplastic concentrations of ascorbic acid, and nitrate reduction.

the best models for predicting O3 and NO(2 )leaf flux were stomatal conductance (g(s)) and symplastic (S) ascorbate (Acs) (R-2 = 0.66) and g(s), apoplastic (A) Acs and NR (R-2=0.89) activity, respectively.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of biochemical processes in determining steady-state leaf-level O(3) (and NO(2)) fluxes.
developing models to explain the variation in leaf-level flux of pollutants such as O(3) or NO(2).
the effects of O(3), NO(2), and SO(2) on the physiology and biochemistry of plants.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
both diffusion and biochemical processes are important in determining leaf fluxes of O(3).
the best-fit model explaining leaf flux of NO(2), stomatal conductance (g(s)), apoplastic aspartate and nitrate reductorase (NR) activity explained 89% and 66% of leaf-level flux of O(3).
the best model explaining NO(3) flux included stomata conductance and apoplastic and ascorbate concentrations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the leaf-level flux of a pollutant gas depends on a number of factors including physical resistance, apoplastic reactions, and symplastic reactions.

the flux of O(3), and to a lesser extent NO(2), into the leaves of C. roseus is determined by the physical resistance of the leaf, the concentration of ascorbate in the symplast and the ability of leaves to remove nitrate generated from NO(2) reactions.

leaf-level fluxes are best explained by models that include stomatal conductance (as a measure of physical resistance), apoplastic and/or symplastic aspartate concentrations (as a measure for biochemical resistance), and NR activity (as a measure to explain the removal rate of the products of reactions of pollutant gases).
The main takeaway from our work is that
fluxes are not only controlled by stomatal conductances, but by other biochemical and physical processes as well.
we can now begin to predict the flux of these gases into leaves based on measurements of a few key parameters.
flux models should include biochemical reactions in addition to the physical resistances.
